newsitem.title: FRANCE: Clinton calls Chirac on NATO, Russia ties.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls Chirac on NATO, Russia ties.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton called French President Jacques Chirac on Thursday to discuss NATO's relations with Russia and a dispute over the alliance's future command structure, the French leader's office said.
Spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said the half-hour telephone call took place in an excellent atmosphere, with a constructive discussion of both issues.

The first conversation between the leaders for more than two months signaled a provisional end to a period of turbulence between Paris and Washington on issues ranging from NATO reform to the United Nations, Africa and the Middle East.

"President Clinton has just called President Chirac to discuss the Atlantic Alliance in its two major components: the prospects for enlargement and relations between the Alliance, Russia and Ukraine just before the president goes to Moscow, and the ongoing reform of the Alliance on which France and the United States now have a wide-ranging dialogue," Colonna said.
She said the two leaders had discussed both issues "in a constructive spirit" and agreed to remain in touch.

Chirac met Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Thursday in Paris and is due to become the first Western leader to see Russian President Boris Yeltsin since his bout of pneumonia when he lunches with the Kremlin leader outside Moscow on Sunday.
In Washington, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had wanted to coordinate positions before the French leader's Moscow trip.
"They talked about the important role that a NATO charter with the Russian Federation will play as we adapt NATO for the future and the challenges of the post-Cold War era," he said.
"It is important, because of the way NATO functions, for the Alliance to operate in harmony and in unison," McCurry said. "We are in a broad sense on the same page."

France wants NATO to agree on a special relationship with Russia in time for an Alliance summit in Madrid in July, which is due to name the first former communist Central European states it aims to admit in 1999.
Moscow strongly opposes NATO enlargement but has agreed to enter talks on closer ties with the 16-nation Western alliance.

There was no indication Chirac and Clinton made progress in substance on a dispute over France's call for the United States to hand over NATO's southern command to a European, on which they had a dissonant exchange of letters last year.
France has made a full return to NATO's military command, which it quit in 1966, conditional on obtaining satisfaction on the "Europeanisation" of the Alliance.

Washington on Tuesday publicly rejected a French compromise proposal to split the Naples-based command, which controls the Mediterranean, giving a U.S. admiral control over air-naval projection forces and a European territorial responsibility.

U.S. officials said there was no sign that most European NATO allies backed such a proposal. Only Germany has backed France's call for a European takeover of AFSOUTH, and diplomats say it has suggested a different compromise under which the post would rotate with the Americans taking it first.

French officials acknowledged that differences still existed but said at least Washington was now talking to France on the issue. Chirac's diplomatic adviser, Jean-David Levitte, held talks at the White House last week with National Security Adviser Alexander Berger.

Some diplomats believe the two sides are so far apart, and the French so isolated, that the only solution could be to postpone the question for review in a few years' time. But it is not clear if that would be enough to persuade Paris to rejoin NATO's military structure.
French officials are now playing down the dispute, saying there is time to find a solution before the Madrid summit, and if not, France will be content to stay where it is.

Chirac faces growing domestic criticism from the left-wing opposition but also some fellow conservatives over his NATO policy, with accusations that he has given away too much without winning any substantial American concessions in return.
